scenarios.name: New menu feedback
scenarios.goal: We changed our menu. I want input on the new dishes, the choices available, and the prices. Find out what customers like and what we should improve.

questions.text: Since the new menu launched last month, have you eaten from it at our restaurant or through an order?
Which new dish or dishes did you try, if you remember?
What did you like most about the new dishes you tried?
What, if anything, would you improve about the new dishes you tried?
How did the portion sizes feel to you: too small, about right, or too large?
How do you feel about the vegetarian choices on the new menu?
How fair did the prices feel for what you received, on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 is not fair at all and 5 is very fair?
Are there any dishes from the old menu that you miss, or anything else you would like us to know?

issues: Q1 screens appropriately, but the questionnaire does not specify whether respondents who answer No/Not sure should skip dish-specific questions or answer only general/menu-awareness questions.
Q6 asks all respondents about vegetarian choices; non-vegetarian customers or those who did not notice the vegetarian section may need an explicit 'not sure/not applicable' option.
Q7 measures overall price fairness well, but it may not distinguish whether prices felt high because of taste, portion size, comparison to old menu, or delivery markups.
improvements: Add interviewer routing after Q1: if Yes, continue; if No/Not sure, skip to a brief awareness/general preferences question or end politely.
For Q6, add probes/options such as: 'If you looked at them, how do you feel about the vegetarian choices—too few, about right, or enough variety? If you did not notice, that is okay.'
Consider adding one short overall satisfaction or revisit-intent question, such as: 'Based on the new menu, how likely are you to order from us again?'
For prices, consider a follow-up open probe: 'What made the prices feel fair or unfair?'

questions.text: Since the new menu launched last month, have you eaten from it at our restaurant or through an order?
Which new dish or dishes did you try, if you remember?
What did you like most about the new dishes you tried?
What, if anything, would you improve about the new dishes you tried?
How did the portion sizes feel to you: too small, about right, or too large?
How do you feel about the vegetarian choices on the new menu?
How fair did the prices feel for what you received, on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 is not fair at all and 5 is very fair?
Are there any dishes from the old menu that you miss, or anything else you would like us to know?

report.headline: Feedback shows many respondents have tried the new menu and appreciate core dishes—especially dal makhani, paneer tikka pasta, and mutton rogan josh—while improvement areas center on value for money, portion size, fewer vegetarian choices, and consistency in spice, sauces, and delivery quality.

themes.title: Core new dishes are landing well on flavor
themes.description: People praised dal makhani for being creamy, thick, rich, smooth, fresh, or comforting; rogan josh for tender meat and aromatic or tasty gravy; and paneer tikka pasta for smoky flavor, seasoning, creaminess, and paneer quality.

quotes.value: Dal was thick and creamy; pasta tasted smoky.
Dal tasted homemade; paneer was soft.
Rogan josh gravy properly thick; meat tender.

themes.title: Paneer and comfort-food qualities are strengths
themes.description: Several people singled out soft, fresh, well-cooked paneer and familiar, homemade, old-style, or family-recipe flavors as positives. This suggests the menu works best when it feels rich and restaurant-quality while still familiar.

quotes.value: Dal tasted homemade; paneer was soft.
Smoky tomato flavor; paneer well cooked.
Creamy texture and paneer pieces; restaurant-level taste.

themes.title: Portions and value are the most repeated pain point
themes.description: Many people said portions or quantities felt too small, often tying that to higher prices or poorer value. The concern appeared across pasta, thali or dal portions, mutton quantity, takeaway portions, and kids’ portions.

quotes.value: Sauce was watery once; portions felt small for the price.
Quantity slightly less than before for the price increase.
Too expensive for the quantity; pasta needed more bite (more spice or thicker sauce).

themes.title: Vegetarian choice feels reduced, with old veg items missed
themes.description: Many people noticed fewer vegetarian choices or said the vegetarian menu feels more limited. Some said the reduction made family ordering harder, and several missed older vegetarian starters, platters, curries, thali components, or mains.

quotes.value: Veg options feel more limited now.
Veg options feel fewer now.
Vegetarian selection okay but options removed; wants more variety.

themes.title: Some still find vegetarian choices acceptable
themes.description: Not all vegetarian feedback was negative: some people said the vegetarian selection is okay, still good, or still varied, and one noted the options felt more premium. Dal makhani and paneer dishes helped carry positive vegetarian impressions.

quotes.value: Vegetarian choices are okay; mother still likes dal makhani.
Vegetarian choices now okay but limited.
It’s okay but fewer options.

themes.title: Consistency issues affect trust in the new dishes
themes.description: People asked for more consistency in sauce thickness, spice distribution, salt, dal or rogan josh thickness, taste, and portion control. This came up both as dish-improvement feedback and as final old-menu or general comments.

quotes.value: Spice wasn’t the same across bites.
Sauce thickness inconsistent—sometimes thick, sometimes watery.
Rogan josh spice uneven (strong then mild); wants more even spice. Dal could be less heavy.

themes.title: Sauce texture and delivery quality need attention
themes.description: Several people mentioned watery, dry, too-thick, or insufficient sauce, especially around paneer tikka pasta and takeaway or delivery. Delivery-specific comments included pasta drying out or arriving watery, and takeaway portions appearing smaller.

quotes.value: Sauce was watery once; portions felt small for the price.
Sauce thickness inconsistent—sometimes thick, sometimes watery.
More sauce; delivery made pasta go dry

themes.title: Some dishes feel too heavy, oily, sweet, sour, or tangy
themes.description: A smaller but repeated set of comments asked for lighter gravies or pasta, less oil, less cheese sauce, or corrections to specific flavor balance issues such as sweetness, sourness, tanginess, and excess capsicum.

quotes.value: Rogan josh spice uneven (strong then mild); wants more even spice. Dal could be less heavy.
Make gravies a bit lighter; add spice-level labels like mild/medium/hot.
Gravies feel heavy—prefer less oil; wants spice-level labels.

themes.title: Menu labels and descriptions are missing useful information
themes.description: People asked for spice-level labels, clearer descriptions of what is spicy versus creamy, and clearer marking of new items. This would help manage expectations, especially because spice and creaminess were both praised and criticized depending on the person.

quotes.value: Make gravies a bit lighter; add spice-level labels like mild/medium/hot.
Gravies feel heavy—prefer less oil; wants spice-level labels.
Menu doesn’t say how spicy things are; kids portions might be small.

themes.title: More key ingredients would make dishes feel more complete
themes.description: Several people wanted more paneer in pasta or starters, more mutton or meat in rogan josh, and more vegetables so the meal feels complete. These comments connect directly to both portion satisfaction and perceived value.

quotes.value: Paneer piece small; veg spread feels smaller than before.
More meat; it’s mostly gravy.
More paneer in the pasta and less tang

sides.position: One person said the portion was too large.
Prices felt fairly good for what was received.
Prices felt unfair or not very fair.
Vegetarian choices are fewer, limited, or not enough.
Vegetarian choices are okay, still varied, good, or more premium.
Some dishes were too hot or should have less spice.
Some dishes needed more spice, more bite, or slightly higher spice.
Some people focused less on heat level and more on making spice consistent.

requests: Increase portion sizes or improve portion value for the price, especially for pasta, thali or dal portions, mutton, takeaway, and kids’ portions.
Bring back or add something similar to old vegetarian starters or platters, including paneer or veg starters suitable for sharing.
Bring back at least one old vegetarian curry, veg main, or old veg thali component.
Add more vegetarian options or mains and more variety overall.
Add spice-level labels and clearer descriptions, including what is spicy versus creamy and which items are new.
Improve consistency in spice, sauce or gravy thickness, salt, taste, and portions.
Improve delivery and takeaway execution so pasta and sauces do not arrive dry or watery and portions look consistent.
Offer a lighter or less oily vegetarian curry or light option.
Add more key ingredients such as paneer, mutton, meat, sauce, or vegetables where people felt dishes were mostly gravy or incomplete.
Adjust prices or make portions larger so the higher menu prices feel matched to what people receive.

gaps.questionText: Which new dish or dishes did you try, if you remember?
What did you like most about the new dishes you tried?
What, if anything, would you improve about the new dishes you tried?
How did the portion sizes feel to you: too small, about right, or too large?
How do you feel about the vegetarian choices on the new menu?
How fair did the prices feel for what you received, on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 is not fair at all and 5 is very fair?
Are there any dishes from the old menu that you miss, or anything else you would like us to know?

nextSteps.suggestion: Review portion standards by dish and channel, starting with paneer tikka pasta, thali dal, mutton rogan josh, takeaway portions, and kids’ portions; consider either increasing quantity or adjusting price where value complaints are strongest.
Add back one or more vegetarian options, prioritizing a shareable veg or paneer starter/platter and one familiar vegetarian curry or thali component.

Keep the flavor direction of the strongest dishes, but tighten recipes and prep specs for dal makhani creaminess, rogan josh thickness and salting, paneer tikka pasta sauce texture, and spice distribution.
Add menu cues for spice level, creaminess, and new items so families and heat-sensitive diners can choose more confidently.
Test lighter variants or a light vegetarian option, using less oil or cheese sauce where appropriate, without losing the creamy qualities people like in dal and paneer dishes.
Audit delivery packaging and hold time for paneer tikka pasta and saucy dishes, because delivery feedback mentioned dryness, watery texture, and smaller-looking takeaway portions.
Increase visible value within dishes by adding key ingredients where feasible, such as more paneer in pasta or starters, more meat in rogan josh, and more vegetables in vegetarian dishes.

issues: Several themes and quotes are not supported by the provided raw-answer sample, including delivery/takeaway packaging issues, pasta arriving dry, old-style/family-recipe flavor, salt, oil, sweetness, sourness, tanginess, excess capsicum, more meat/mutton, kids' portions being small, and 'premium' vegetarian options.

The report presents precise people counts that cannot be verified from the sample and often exceed the visible evidence. In the provided sample, there are only 8 responses per question, while the report claims themes with 10, 12, 15, or 16 people and disagreement totals such as 14/11/6/1 for portions.

Some quoted evidence appears fabricated or at least absent from the sample, e.g. 'Rogan josh tasted close to old-style; meat tender,' 'Need more quantity; felt reduced while price was higher,' 'More sauce; delivery made pasta go dry,' and 'Takeaway portions sometimes look smaller; improve packaging or portion control.'
The report over-fragments the findings into overlapping themes: value/portions, key ingredients, sauce texture, and delivery quality partially repeat the same small set of visible comments.
The gaps section may be based on the full survey logic, but it is not checkable from the supplied sample and gives a false sense of precision without stating that the reviewer only has a sample.
The headline mentions 'delivery quality,' but the supplied sample does not show delivery-quality feedback; it only includes restaurant/order/takeaway context and one comment about portions/labels.
missed_patterns: Customers had some uncertainty about whether they had tried the new menu; one respondent was 'Not sure' and another was not fully sure the rogan josh item was new. Clear 'new' labels are therefore especially important.
Price fairness in the visible sample is mixed-to-negative, with ratings 4,3,2,4,2,1,3,3 averaging about 2.75; the report captures value concerns but could state the visible ratings more directly.

The thali is a specific issue: it was described as slightly pricey, missing an old veg curry/thali component, and centered on dal/paneer. The report mentions thali but does not isolate it as a menu-format improvement opportunity.
Family/household vegetarian needs appear in the sample through comments about a mother, wife, kids, and families; the report touches on family ordering but could make this more actionable.
strengths: The main high-level story is accurate for the provided sample: dal makhani, paneer tikka pasta, and mutton rogan josh are liked, while value, portion size, vegetarian variety, and consistency are the main concerns.
The report includes strong, practical next steps that generally follow from the evidence: review portion standards, restore vegetarian options, tighten recipes, and add clearer menu labels.
The vegetarian-choice issue is well captured, including both reduced variety and missed old veg items such as veg kebab/platter/curry options.
The report correctly identifies consistency problems around spice distribution and sauce/gravy thickness, which recur clearly in the raw answers.
The headline is readable and mostly accurate apart from the unsupported delivery-quality phrase.

asks.question: Which dishes got the most criticism and why?
asks.answer: Among the people who answered with dish-specific criticism, paneer tikka pasta appears to have drawn the most repeated complaints: portions/value, not enough paneer, sauce or delivery texture problems, and flavor balance issues like too tangy, too cheesy/heavy, too sweet, needing more spice, or needing more char. [e210, e221, e224, e229, e243, e248, e250, e253, e256, e260, e262, e265, e266, e269, e335] Mutton rogan josh was another common target, mainly for inconsistent spice, wanting more meat or a bigger portion, and gravy issues such as too sour, oily, thick, or under-salted. [e211, e218, e223, e233, e236, e243, e256, e262, e481] Dal makhani and thali items got criticism too, especially that dal/thali portions felt smaller, the dal could be heavy or sweet, and some customers missed the older dal or old thali/veg components. [e211, e217, e225, e230, e251, e489, e497, e523] Separately from specific dishes, vegetarian choices were a broad complaint: several customers said there are fewer veg options or asked for old veg starters/curries/platter items to return. [e341, e343, e346, e347, e361, e365, e399, e406, e477, e479, e482, e483, e484, e486]

asks.question: Are the price complaints about the price itself or the portion size?
asks.answer: The price complaints appear to be mostly about portion/value, not just the sticker price: customers repeatedly said portions or quantity felt small for the price or after the price increase (e205, e209, e210, e213, e214, e217, e223, e225, e227, e229, e248, e266, e272). There are a few broader price-only or pricing-adjustment comments, such as the thali feeling slightly pricey or wanting pricing to better match what is received, but these are often still tied to portion or filling value (e207, e248, e499, e520). So the strongest improvement signal is to increase portions/quantity or improve perceived value if prices stay higher, rather than only lowering prices (e482, e489, e499, e520).
